title: The Distinction of Divinity and Humanity
english: If someone says: 'For this reason I am rational, because I have a rational father; and for this reason I am mortal, because I have a mortal father,' it is true; for the 'because' is a demonstrative cause. Since, therefore, he lives because of the father, what is being said is not a life named from life, but as a fountain of life and as one giving to all; for we say that the living one has life, but we also say that the life is not one named from life, for life does not participate in [something else], but it is life itself. Thus, he does not live through the father.

A human, therefore, [lives] because of something, but God [is] not because of something. Yet both have run together regarding the arrival of a season. I do not say the arrival is entirely according to the flesh; for many [seasons] He desired; He is always arriving. And thus I have drawn out what is in Micah: 'And you, Bethlehem, house of Ephrathah, you are small. Out of you shall come to me the ruler, and his exits are from the beginning' (Micah 5:2). For it is not that he came from the father just now previously, from which the need of the administration of saving things [comes]. The need of his exit is always happening and happening wherever. For this reason, he said not one, but many exits. 'For this reason He will give them until the time of birthing.'

The last exit, that of the birthing of Mary, is a certain 'until the time of birthing'; for the Scripture does not praise those [plural] birthing, but says one birthing, signified by the word. And 'birthing' in the strict sense is not one who took in seed and conceived and formed and surrounded, but she herself gives birth. For this reason, he came from a woman. No one of the others [comes] from a woman, but all [come] through a woman; yet all [come] from men; for the woman comes from the man, and the man through the woman. And this must be said: that genealogies are made casually, scientifically, and piously when they are descended from fathers; for the genealogy from women is slandered. Therefore, only this one has given birth without a man. And for this reason the Savior came from a woman, not through a woman, even if many others are made [to be said] not 'from Mary,' but 'through Mary.' So many will seem to be ambassadors [speaking thus]. And God is from the Father and not because of something, but the human...

Regarding the descent from David and Mary and for what reason: for the sake of the salvation of the world he has come, to abolish death, to do much for mortals who had cast [themselves] away through their own negligence. Why do I say these things in grace? The things said about the Savior declare his divinity. And all the things reported concerning divinity are incomparable to any other; for he is the only-begotten. But the things said about the man touch upon human faults, just as they do those of the dying. The zealous become imitators of the man. But they do not imitate the divinity—for this is an unreasonableness—they imitate the man. Whatever is said about the man could also be said about the angels and about perfect men. But whatever is said about the divinity, neither about angels nor about holy men will be said. I do not say that any of the created things is wisdom, or a radiance of glory, or a character of the divine essence, or the only-begotten Son of God.

But whatever is said as being about the man, it could be said, for example: 'You seek to kill me, a man,' being 'one who has spoken the truth to you, which I heard from God' (John 8:46). And many others, having learned the truth from God, spoke the truth. Not this one more, but this one more, this one incomparably. And again: 'But because I tell you the truth, you do not believe me' (John 14:11). And others speak the truth: for if we grant that no one spoke the truth except Christ himself, we give in to the anonymous heresy. That is, an anonymous heresy that seems to overturn [the truth] or to have come from the books. And many have books and compositions, and they say this too: that the truth never came among men except upon the appearance of the Savior; for 'grace and truth came through Jesus Christ' (John 1:17). And see where the argument leads them: because they want the old scripture to not be from God, nor the prophets, they say that the truth never came to men except after the appearance having happened. And saying these things, they divide the one divinity, and they say that the one who was the Creator was before the appearance, and they seek another father for Christ. But we do not say this, that ever the truth...

title: The Eternity of Christ's Reign
english: It has been hidden. It always sends out its own testimonies. Among men, however, it is a matter of either seeing it or not seeing it. And just as it happens to the perceptible sun that those with clouded eyes cannot see it, and we do not immediately say that the sun does not exist, so also we do not say that truth has never existed among men, lest we should disparage the Scripture.

And I say to you: if you bring me two different kinds of fruits, such as figs, because you divided them from the matter, it is necessary that other plants and other things also be. Therefore, it is impossible for the Gospel instruction to have made the truth into men, nor for the one called the old before the advent to have been enlightened according to the truth. They necessarily approached from different fruits and different qualities; not because there is a different divinity, but because of their strange beginning, this followed.

If, therefore, the Savior says: 'I am the truth' (John 14:6) and Shepherd and Door and the others, these names and what is signified by them are unshared from the natural ones. But if he says that 'I am a man', if it is said about him that he is righteous—'you killed the righteous one,' says Peter (Acts 7:52)—these names run together for both men and angels.

Take the same manner for me regarding a king; and since a king is something of a nature with the kingdom of the Word, unable to be either taken up or cast off, that itself is kingdom. And just as one is not called righteous because he possesses righteousness, but being righteousness itself, so also a king is not from appointment, but the king himself is from the King, as God is from God. He also has an acquired kingship, which he desired to have by appearing, so that he might also bring down those warring against the human race and bring them themselves into a lawful dominion, so that he might rule lawfully.

If, therefore, he says: 'I have been established king by him upon his holy Mount Zion' (Psalm 2:6), he is not speaking about the innate and eternal kingship, but about that which he received for our sake. And teaching is a kingship upon God. Thus, there was the teaching before the advent, which they said was spoken by him as a Word like God, and there is another for the sake of some. This, therefore, has a beginning and an end. For it has been said in...

To the twelve prophets: 'and the Lord shall reign from Zion from now and until the age'. The 'from' and 'until' signify time. But if it is said concerning a man that he reigns from this time and until that, it signifies a limited [reign]; for before the time from which his kingship began, he was not king, and at the end of the kingship, he is no longer king.

But concerning the Savior we do not say this, rather he reigned from the time from which he received authority through ordination, and he is no longer reigning when this reaches an end; for that [end] is through him. Just as divinity does not come to him through another, so neither does the kingship nor the holiness. 'God is our king before the age' (Ps 89:3). And the kingship before the age is through him.

Again: 'your kingdom is the kingdom of all the ages' (Rev 11:15). This is said of the Word God. The Word has neither a beginning having kingship nor an ending; for 'Lord' [means] 'reigning for the age and upon the age and yet more'. He was at a loss to signify [the difference between] time and age, and said 'and yet more'. We take 'yet more' thus: even if you take another age, he reigns yet more; even if another, yet more; even if all [ages], yet more he reigns; from which it is shown that his beginning is without end; for the kingship which he had according to [human] kingship has sometimes ceased and has taken a beginning; but why is [this kingship]? Because of the salvation of the world, because of the removal of 'the sin of the world' (John 1:29).

And just as a physician is always a physician from the time he has the art, and as far as he practices it, he has a beginning and an end of being a physician, and for the one suffering, there is a beginning and an end of that physician being 'yet more', when he reaches a possible health and a possible recovery, so also you will say concerning teachers. There is a certain teacher from whom one has received knowledge. He becomes a teacher of this [one] when he comes to him; and when that one has been instructed and has fully taken up the knowledge like the teacher, he ceases to be his teacher. And it is a kind of virtue for a teacher to sometimes cease to be a teacher of this [one]; for having perfected them, he is no longer [their teacher]. But if he remains always a teacher of this [one], no one is perfected according to the teaching of him. Therefore, hearing such things, those not understanding the Scriptures in this way—for example:

title: The Kingly Joy and Reward
english: "When the kingdom is handed over to God and Father," he no longer reigns in the same way; not that he ceases to reign entirely, but he no longer reigns thus. There, he is called both king and kingdom; for "Lord, the king shall rejoice in your power" (Ps 21:13). If we take this word regarding the Word of God, he himself is found to be both king and power; for "Christ is the power of God" (1 Cor 1:24), and "the power of the Most High"—who is this?—"overshadowed" (Luke 1:35) Mary, so that she might conceive and become the mother of the temple. Therefore, if we wish to receive power from the Word of God, we look for the king, the Lordly man. He rejoices in the power of God.

Has the success not occurred in those things in which it is necessary to rejoice and be glad? These successes have not happened by the power of the man, but from the power to the man. Likewise, Paul says the resurrection of the Savior happens in this way: "He was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God" (2 Cor 4:10). We do not say the life is living by the power of God, nor the power is living by the power of God. "Having been put to death in the flesh, he was made alive in the spirit." He is put to death in the flesh, not put to death in divinity. We understand these things said about the man because: "the king shall rejoice in your power" (Ps 21:13); for even if he has prevailed over wars and subjected them and "given authority to tread upon serpents and scorpions" (Luke 10:19), this has happened by power; for this power strengthened the existing temple and the king himself to become the "author of salvation" (Acts 3:15).

"You put to death the author of life" (Acts 3:15). He is first in all things; for he says, "so that he might become himself first in all things." He is second to no one, nor is anyone equal to him in common things. I say, then, that the affairs of the Lordly man and the holy men are common. But no one is equal to him, nor is he second to anyone; therefore he is called the leader. "Lord, the king shall rejoice in your power" (Ps 21:13). And this could be said of each individual queen according to God. Abraham was a private person regarding his immediate life, yet it is said he was a "king by God." Thus, he had another kingdom: to save the divine laws and the spiritual [things].

For he who reigns thus, even if he does not rule others, rules himself; first himself, then others. Again: 'You have reigned without us; and it would have been better if you had also reigned, so that we too might reign with you.' Do not think, O Corinthians—for they were self-willed in this and thought greatly of themselves—he says: do not think that we envy you if you reign. We do not reign for your sake. God does not wish to complete us without you; for this reason we do not reign because you are not yet reigning. If, therefore, you reign, we are ready to reign.

Just as if certain people, being great men, were called to a banquet by the king. The philanthropy of the king called also those inferior to those present. He says: 'Let us not eat without them, so that they might not be left out, those coming later, to be feasted.' They also have those who arrived beforehand and were feasting previously. This also is said in Psalm 1: 'The righteous shall wait for me, until I repay them in kind' (Psalm 1:5). No one is said to wait by chance among those expecting to wait, but rather the one who has received [the call], having a purpose to enjoy these things.

Every one of the saints, therefore, is a king. And they were saying that what is fitting for the Savior also fits the righteous, even if in a diminished and lesser way. He says therefore also concerning each saint: 'Lord, in your power the king shall be made glad.' And he did not say 'he rejoices,' but 'he shall be made glad.' When the time of gladness is, then he shall be made glad.

4 Therefore, this can also be said specifically concerning David and concerning his human and sensible kingship, that having ruled the kingdom well, he shall receive a reward upon it; for each one, when he has been entrusted with what, if he endures well, has a reward upon them. Becoming faithful over a little, he enters 'into the joy' (Matthew 25:21) of the neighbor and of God. 2 Lord, in your power the king shall be made glad. He speaks of the saving power that makes the king rejoice, according to how God is the Word. Previously it was said that the words must be taken just as the underlying things are, and not to force the things toward the meaning. With us, the name of power is being worn down. It signifies many things; I say power as equal to strength. I do not say thus the Savior of God...
